intro: Look around the room. The door is a rectangle. Its corners are right angles. The floor tiles line up in rows that never cross. A slice of pizza is a triangle with a sharp point. Every object you can see is built from points, lines, angles and shapes, and each one has a name and a rule. In this unit you learn those names and rules, and you learn to measure an angle with a protractor the way a city planner or a carpenter does.

Then you learn to say exactly where something is. A treasure map says the X is at (7, 4), and two numbers are enough to find one spot on a whole field. That grid, the coordinate plane, does more than locate things. When you save $3 a week and plot your savings, the points line up in a straight row. Patterns turn into pictures.

By the end you will sort triangles and quadrilaterals by their properties, explain why every square is a rectangle, find lines of symmetry, plot and name points, measure distances along a grid, and make and describe number patterns from a rule. These are the tools of maps, buildings, games and graphs.
bigQuestion: How do angles, shapes and coordinates let us describe the world exactly enough to build it, map it and find our way through it?

timeline.t: Babylonian astronomers count in 60s, the root of our 360-degree circle
Euclid's Elements defines points, lines and angles and proves facts about triangles
Eratosthenes uses the angle of a shadow to estimate the size of the Earth
René Descartes links algebra and geometry; coordinate grids are later called Cartesian after him
The Land Ordinance sets up a grid survey for public land, including the future Illinois
Surveyors lay out Illinois in square townships and mile-wide sections, a grid you can still see from the air
James Thompson's plat maps Chicago's first streets as a grid of blocks
Chicago numbers its addresses from State and Madison, making the city one giant coordinate plane
Daniel Burnham's Plan of Chicago proposes diagonal boulevards cutting across the grid
GPS gives every place on Earth two coordinates, latitude and longitude

words.d: a straight path with one endpoint that goes on forever in one direction
two rays with a shared endpoint; its size is the amount of turn between them
the unit for angle size; a full turn is 360°
an angle of exactly 90°, a square corner
an angle less than 90°
an angle more than 90° and less than 180°
lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet
lines that cross at a right angle
a closed shape with four straight sides
a line you can fold a shape along so the halves match exactly
two numbers (x, y) that name a point: over x, then up y
an instruction that makes a pattern, like 'start at 5, add 4'

test.q: One side of an angle sits on the 0 of the inside scale. The other side reads 40 on the inside scale and 140 on the outside. The angle looks smaller than a square corner. What is its measure?
test.why: Use the scale that started at 0, and 40° matches an angle smaller than 90°.

test.q: An angle measures 45°. What kind of angle is it?
test.why: 45 is less than 90, so it is acute.

test.q: A 90° angle is split into a 40° angle and one other angle. What is the other angle?
Which lines never meet, no matter how far they go?
test.why: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart everywhere.

test.q: A triangle has angles 90°, 45° and 45°, and two equal sides. What is it?
test.why: Two equal sides make it isosceles, and the 90° angle makes it a right triangle.
A square has four equal sides, which is the rule for a rhombus.

test.q: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 100°, 80° and 100°. What is the fourth angle?
How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle that is not a square have?
test.why: One line through the middles of the long sides and one through the middles of the short sides. The diagonals do not work.

test.q: To plot (6, 2), start at the origin and
test.why: The first number is x (right) and the second is y (up).

test.q: What is the distance from (2, 7) to (9, 7)?
test.why: Same y, so subtract the x-coordinates: 9 − 2 = 7.

test.q: Rule: start at 3, add 7. What is the 5th term?
Pattern A adds 2 from 0 and pattern B adds 8 from 0. At step 6, A is 12 and B is 48. What rule connects B to A at every step?
test.why: 8 is 4 times 2, so B is always 4 times A: 12 × 4 = 48.

test.q: Three corners of a rectangle are (1, 1), (7, 1) and (7, 5). What is its perimeter?
Which point lies on the x-axis?
test.why: A point on the x-axis has gone up 0, so its y-coordinate is 0.

write.prompt: Three corners of a rectangle are at (2, 1), (9, 1) and (9, 6). Find the fourth corner, the width, the height and the perimeter, and explain each step. Then explain, using the rules for the shapes, why every square is a rectangle but not every rectangle is a square.
tips: State each answer clearly: the fourth corner, the width, the height, the perimeter.
Show the subtraction you used for each length and say which coordinates you subtracted and why.
Check the perimeter by adding the four sides in a different order.
For the square and rectangle question, write the rule for each shape and test it both ways.

title: Geometry and the Coordinate Plane

chapters.title: Angles, Lines and Shapes
chapters.bigQuestion: How do lines and angles let us describe and sort every shape we see?

story.title: The Planner's Map
story.kicker: A city planner looks at a map of Chicago and sees angles on every corner.
paragraphs: Maya's aunt is a city planner. Her office has a big map of Chicago on the wall. Most streets run straight north and south or straight east and west. Where they cross, they make square corners. Maya's aunt says the whole city is built on a grid, like a sheet of graph paper.

Then Maya notices some streets that break the pattern. Milwaukee Avenue cuts across the grid at a slant. So do Clark Street, Lincoln Avenue and Archer Avenue. Her aunt says those roads follow old trails that were there before the grid was drawn. Where a slanted street meets a straight one, the corners are not square. One corner is narrow and sharp. The corner across from it is wide and open.

Her aunt hands her a clear plastic half circle with numbers around the edge. She calls it a protractor and says it measures how open a corner is. Maya lays it on a corner where two grid streets meet. The line hits 90. She tries a corner where Milwaukee Avenue crosses a grid street. That one reads close to 45. Same city, different angles.

Planners need these numbers. A sharp corner is hard for a bus to turn. A lot on a slanted street has a strange shape for a building. Every street, every lot and every park is made of lines and angles. This chapter gives you the names and the tools that planners use. Soon you will see the angles in your own neighborhood.
story.think: Why might a city planner care whether two streets meet at a square corner or a slanted one?

lessons.title: Points, Lines, Rays and Segments
lessons.mainIdea: Geometry starts with points, and lines, rays and segments are the straight paths that connect them.
reading: Touch the tip of your pencil to paper and lift it. That dot is a *point*. A point has a location but no size. We name points with capital letters, like point A. Now draw a straight path through A that goes on forever in both directions. That is a *line*. A line has no ends. We draw arrows on both sides to show it keeps going. We name a line by two points on it, like line AB.

Most straight things we see do not go on forever. A crosswalk stripe starts and stops. That is a *line segment*, a piece of a line with two endpoints. Segment AB has endpoint A and endpoint B, and it has a length you can measure. A *ray* is different. It starts at one endpoint and goes on forever in one direction, like the beam from a flashlight. Ray AB starts at A and passes through B.

Here is a quick way to tell them apart. Count the endpoints. Zero endpoints: a line. One endpoint: a ray. Two endpoints: a segment. A common mistake is to name a ray backward. Ray AB and ray BA are not the same, because the first letter must be the endpoint. Ray AB starts at A. Ray BA starts at B and heads the other way.

words.d: an exact location with no size, shown as a dot and named with a capital letter
a straight path that goes on forever in both directions, with no endpoints
a piece of a line with two endpoints and a length you can measure
a straight path with one endpoint that goes on forever in one direction

look.title: Three Paths on a Map
look.text: Picture a map of a town. A railroad track runs straight across the whole map and off both edges. A crosswalk goes from one curb to the other curb. A searchlight at the airport shines a straight beam up into the night sky. Each of these is like one of the figures you just read about.
look.prompt: Name each path as a line, a segment or a ray, and say how many endpoints each one has.

check.q: Which figure has exactly one endpoint?
check.why: A ray starts at one endpoint and goes on forever in one direction. A line has no endpoints and a segment has two.

check.q: Ray CD starts at which point?
check.why: The first letter in a ray's name is its endpoint, so ray CD starts at C and passes through D.

check.q: A student draws a straight path with an arrow on each end. What did the student draw?
check.why: Arrows on both ends mean the path goes on forever both ways, which is a line.

lessons.title: What an Angle Is
lessons.mainIdea: An angle is two rays that share an endpoint, and its size is how far open they are, not how long they are.
reading: Open a book partway. The two covers meet at the spine. That opening is an *angle*. In geometry, an angle is made of two rays that share the same endpoint. The shared endpoint is the *vertex*. The two rays are the sides. We name an angle with three points and put the vertex in the middle. Angle ABC has its vertex at B.

The size of an angle is the amount of turn between its two sides. Think of a clock. At 3:00 the hands make a square corner. At 1:00 the hands are close together, a small opening. Angle size is measured in *degrees*. A full turn all the way around is 360 degrees, written 360°. A square corner is one quarter of a full turn: 360 ÷ 4 = 90°. Half a turn, a straight line, is 180°.

The most common mistake is to think a longer side means a bigger angle. It does not. Draw a small V and a giant V with the same opening. Both angles are the same size, because the turn between the sides is the same. Only the opening counts. If you stretch the sides of a 40° angle to twice their length, it is still a 40° angle.

words.d: two rays that share an endpoint; its size is how far apart the rays are turned
the shared endpoint of an angle's two sides; the middle letter in the angle's name
the unit for angle size; a full turn is 360 degrees, written 360°

look.title: The Pizza Slice
look.text: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. Every slice is an angle with its vertex at the center of the pizza. The whole pizza is a full turn, 360°. To find the angle of one slice, divide: 360 ÷ 8 = 45°. Now picture a pizza cut into 6 equal slices instead, and another cut into 12.
look.prompt: How many degrees is one slice of the 6-slice pizza? How many degrees is one slice of the 12-slice pizza?

check.q: In angle PQR, which point is the vertex?
check.why: The vertex is always the middle letter in an angle's name, so the vertex is Q.

check.q: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. How many degrees is each slice?
check.why: 360 ÷ 4 = 90. Four square corners fill a full turn.

check.q: Angle A has sides 2 cm long and measures 30°. Angle B has sides 10 cm long and also measures 30°. Which is true?
check.why: Angle size is the amount of turn between the sides. Side length does not change it, so both are 30°.

lessons.title: Measuring With a Protractor
lessons.mainIdea: Line up the vertex and one side, then read the scale that starts at 0 on that side.
reading: A *protractor* is a half-circle tool marked from 0 to 180 degrees. Most protractors have two *scales*, one running left to right and one right to left. To measure an angle, follow three steps. Step 1: put the small hole or dot at the center of the protractor exactly on the vertex. Step 2: turn the protractor so one side of the angle lies along the 0 line. Step 3: find where the other side crosses the curved edge and read the number.

The two scales cause most mistakes. Suppose one side sits on the 0 mark of the inside scale. The other side crosses the edge where the inside scale says 50 and the outside scale says 130. Which is right? Use the scale that started at 0 on your first side. That gives 50°. Now check with your eyes. Does the angle look smaller than a square corner? If yes, the answer must be less than 90, so 50° makes sense and 130° does not.

Sometimes the sides of a drawn angle are too short to reach the edge of the protractor. Extend them with a *straightedge*. Making a side longer does not change the angle. You can also draw an angle. To draw a 65° angle, draw a ray first. Put the center on its endpoint, mark a dot at 65 on the correct scale, and connect the endpoint to the dot.

words.d: a half-circle tool marked in degrees, used to measure and draw angles
a row of numbers on a measuring tool; a protractor has two, one in each direction
any tool with a straight edge, like a ruler, used to draw or extend a line

look.title: Angles Between the Clock Hands
look.cite: A clock face: 360° ÷ 12 hour marks = 30° per hour mark
look.prompt: How many degrees are between the hands at 5 o'clock? How do you know without measuring?

check.q: One side of an angle sits on the 0 of the inside scale. The other side lines up with 70 on the inside scale and 110 on the outside. The angle looks smaller than a square corner. What is its measure?
check.why: Read the scale that started at 0 on the first side. Also, 70° is less than 90°, which matches how the angle looks.

check.q: What is the first step in measuring an angle with a protractor?
choices: Read the biggest number on the edge
Measure the length of one side
Lay the protractor on the longest side
Put the center mark on the vertex
check.why: The center mark must sit exactly on the vertex, or every reading will be off.

check.q: At 4 o'clock, how many degrees are between the clock hands?
check.why: Each hour mark is 360 ÷ 12 = 30°, and 4 × 30 = 120.

lessons.title: Right, Acute and Obtuse
lessons.mainIdea: Compare an angle to a square corner: less than 90° is acute, exactly 90° is right, more than 90° is obtuse.
reading: A square corner, like the corner of a sheet of paper, is a *right angle*. It measures exactly 90°. We mark a right angle with a small square drawn in the corner. Any angle smaller than a right angle is an *acute angle*. Acute angles are sharp and narrow, between 0° and 90°. The tip of a pizza slice is acute. Any angle bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight line is an *obtuse angle*, between 90° and 180°.

Sort these angles: 35°, 90°, 125°, 89°, 91°. The 35° and 89° angles are acute, because they are less than 90. The 90° angle is right. The 125° and 91° angles are obtuse, because they are more than 90 but less than 180. Notice that 89° and 91° look almost the same. That is why a protractor matters. A *straight angle* is exactly 180°. Its two sides form a straight line.

A common mistake is to guess from how the drawing is turned. An obtuse angle that opens downward is still obtuse. Another mistake is calling any big-looking angle a right angle. Use the corner of an index card as a test. If the card fits exactly, the angle is right. If the card covers more than the angle, the angle is acute. If the angle is wider than the card, the angle is obtuse.

words.d: an angle of exactly 90°, a square corner, marked with a small square
an angle smaller than a right angle, between 0° and 90°
an angle bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight line, between 90° and 180°
an angle of exactly 180°; its two sides make a straight line

look.title: Corners of the Letters
look.text: Look at capital letters. The letter L has one corner where the two strokes meet. The letter V has one corner at the bottom. The letter A has a corner at the top and two more where the crossbar meets the sides. The letter T has two corners where the top meets the stem. Compare each corner to the corner of an index card.
look.prompt: Which of these letters have right angles, and which have acute angles? Where in the letter A would you find an obtuse angle?

check.q: An angle measures 112°. What kind of angle is it?
check.why: 112 is more than 90 and less than 180, so it is obtuse.

check.q: Which of these angles is acute?
check.why: Acute angles are less than 90°, and 72 is the only choice below 90.

check.q: The corner of an index card fits inside an angle with room left over. What kind of angle is it?
check.why: The angle is wider than the card's 90° corner, so it is obtuse.

lessons.title: Adding and Splitting Angles
lessons.mainIdea: When a ray splits an angle into two parts, the two parts add up to the whole angle.
reading: Angles add just like lengths. Picture a 90° corner. Draw a ray from the vertex through the middle of it. Now there are two smaller angles. If one is 30°, the other must be 90 − 30 = 60°. Together, 30 + 60 = 90, the whole corner. Angle measure is *additive*: the parts add up to the *whole angle*. This lets you find a missing angle without measuring it.

Try this one. Angle ABC is 140°. Ray BD splits it into angle ABD and angle DBC. Angle ABD measures 55°. What is angle DBC? Subtract: 140 − 55 = 85°. Check by adding: 55 + 85 = 140. It works. The same idea works on a straight line. The angles along a straight line add to 180°. If one angle on the line is 110°, the other is 180 − 110 = 70°.

Two mistakes are common. One is subtracting from 90 when the whole angle is 180, or from 180 when the whole is 90. Always ask first: what is the whole? The other is subtracting the wrong way, like 55 − 140. The part is always smaller than the whole, so subtract the part from the whole. When two parts are equal, divide the whole by 2. A 90° corner split into two equal angles gives 45° each.

words.d: made by adding; angle measures are additive because the parts add up to the whole
the full angle before it is split into parts; the parts must add up to it

look.title: The Split Corner
look.text: A carpenter cuts a 90° corner of a board with one straight cut from the vertex. One of the two new angles measures 38°. The other angle is the rest of the corner: 90 − 38 = 52°. Check: 38 + 52 = 90. Now suppose the carpenter instead cuts a straight 180° edge, and one of the two new angles is 38°.
look.prompt: What is the other angle when the whole is 180°? Explain the subtraction you used and check it by adding.

check.q: A 90° angle is split into two parts. One part is 25°. What is the other part?
Two angles together make a straight line. One is 135°. What is the other?
check.why: A straight angle is 180°, and 180 − 135 = 45.

check.q: Angle XYZ is 120°. Ray YW splits it into two equal angles. How big is each one?
check.why: Equal parts of 120 are 120 ÷ 2 = 60 each, and 60 + 60 = 120.

lessons.title: Parallel and Perpendicular
lessons.mainIdea: Parallel lines never meet and stay the same distance apart; perpendicular lines meet at right angles.
reading: Look at railroad tracks. The two rails run side by side and never touch, no matter how far they go. Lines like this are *parallel*. Parallel lines stay the same distance apart everywhere. On a map of Chicago, most north-south streets are parallel to each other, and most east-west streets are parallel to each other. We write that line AB is parallel to line CD with the symbol ∥.

Now look at where a north-south street crosses an east-west street. They meet at a square corner, a right angle. Lines that cross at 90° are *perpendicular*. The symbol is ⊥. The edges of a door, a window or a page are perpendicular where they meet. Two lines can also cross without being perpendicular. A slanted street crossing a grid street makes one acute and one obtuse angle, so those lines *intersect* but are not perpendicular.

A common mistake is to think lines that do not cross on the page are parallel. Two lines can be slightly tilted and cross far off the page. Real parallel lines never cross, so check that the distance between them is the same at both ends. Another mistake is calling any crossing lines perpendicular. Check for the square corner. Perpendicular lines always intersect, but intersecting lines are not always perpendicular.

words.d: lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet, like railroad rails
lines that cross at a right angle, 90°, like the edges of a page
to cross; two lines intersect at the one point they share

look.title: Streets on the Grid
look.text: On a grid map, Main Street runs east and west. Oak Street also runs east and west, two blocks north of Main. Elm Street runs north and south and crosses both. A fourth road, Old Trail Road, cuts across all three at a slant. Think about each pair of roads and the angles where they meet.
look.prompt: Which pair of streets is parallel? Which pairs are perpendicular? Which roads intersect Old Trail Road, and are those crossings perpendicular?

check.q: Two lines cross and form four right angles. The lines are
check.why: Lines that cross at 90° are perpendicular by definition.

check.q: Which statement is always true of parallel lines?
check.why: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart everywhere, so they never meet.

check.q: Two streets cross at a slant, making 60° and 120° angles. What are the streets?
check.why: They cross, so they intersect, but the angles are not 90°, so they are not perpendicular.

lessons.title: Sorting Triangles
lessons.mainIdea: Sort a triangle two ways: by its sides (how many are equal) and by its biggest angle (right, acute or obtuse).
reading: A triangle has three straight sides and three angles. Look at its sides first. If all three sides are the same length, it is *equilateral*. A yield sign is one. If exactly two sides are equal, it is *isosceles*. If no sides are equal, it is *scalene*. Tick marks on a drawing show which sides are equal. Sides with the same number of ticks are the same length.

Now look at the angles. A triangle can have at most one right angle or one obtuse angle. If one angle is exactly 90°, it is a *right triangle*. If one angle is more than 90°, it is an obtuse triangle. If all three angles are less than 90°, it is an acute triangle. A triangle gets both names at once. A triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm and one 90° corner is a scalene right triangle.

A helpful fact: the three angles of any triangle add up to 180°. So if two angles are 50° and 60°, the third is 180 − 50 − 60 = 70°, and the triangle is acute. Common mistake: calling a tipped triangle a different kind. Turn the page; the sides and angles do not change. Another: thinking an equilateral triangle can have a right angle. It cannot, because 180 ÷ 3 = 60, so all three of its angles are 60°.

words.d: a triangle with all three sides the same length; all its angles are 60°
a triangle with exactly two sides the same length
a triangle with no equal sides
a triangle with one 90° angle

look.title: Triangle Angle Sums
look.cite: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°
look.prompt: A triangle has angles of 35° and 55°. What is the third angle, and what kind of triangle is it?

check.q: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. What kind is it by its sides?
check.why: Exactly two sides are equal, which makes it isosceles.

check.q: Two angles of a triangle are 40° and 30°. What is the third angle?
check.why: 180 − 40 − 30 = 110, so the third angle is 110°, and the triangle is obtuse.

check.q: Why can a triangle never have two right angles?
choices: Two right angles already use all 180°, leaving nothing for the third angle
Right angles only fit in squares
A triangle has only two angles
check.why: 90 + 90 = 180, the whole sum, so the third angle would have to be 0°, which is impossible.

lessons.title: Quadrilateral Families
lessons.mainIdea: Quadrilaterals are sorted by asking three questions: which sides are parallel, which sides are equal, and which angles are right angles.
reading: A *quadrilateral* is any closed shape with four straight sides. Its four angles always add up to 360°. Sort quadrilaterals by asking three questions. Are any sides parallel? Are any sides equal? Are any angles right angles? A *trapezoid* has at least one pair of parallel sides. A *parallelogram* has two pairs of parallel sides, and its opposite sides are equal.

Inside the parallelogram family are three famous shapes. A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles. A *rhombus* is a parallelogram with four equal sides, like a tilted diamond. A square is a parallelogram with four right angles and four equal sides. A kite is different. It has two pairs of equal sides that sit next to each other, not across from each other, and it is not a parallelogram.

Try sorting. Shape 1 has sides 4, 6, 4, 6 and four right angles: a rectangle. Shape 2 has four sides of 5 and no right angles: a rhombus. Shape 3 has only one pair of parallel sides: a trapezoid. Common mistake: thinking a tilted square is a rhombus but not a square. Turning a shape does not change it. If it has four equal sides and four right angles, it is a square, however it sits.

words.d: a closed shape with four straight sides; its angles add up to 360°
a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides
a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides; opposite sides are equal
a parallelogram with four equal sides

look.title: Sort the Signs
look.text: Four street signs are cut from metal. Sign A: four sides, each 60 cm, and four square corners. Sign B: four sides of 60 cm, but pushed over so the corners are 70° and 110°. Sign C: top 40 cm, bottom 80 cm, top and bottom parallel, the two slanted sides equal. Sign D: sides of 60 cm and 90 cm, with four square corners.
look.prompt: Give each sign its most specific name: square, rhombus, rectangle or trapezoid. Which of the signs are parallelograms?

check.q: A quadrilateral has four equal sides and no right angles. Its most specific name is
check.why: Four equal sides make a rhombus; without right angles it is not a square.

check.q: A quadrilateral has only one pair of parallel sides. What is it?
check.why: A parallelogram, a rectangle and a rhombus all have two pairs of parallel sides. Only a trapezoid can have just one pair.

check.q: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 90°, 90° and 120°. What is the fourth angle?
check.why: The four angles total 360°: 360 − 90 − 90 − 120 = 60.

lessons.title: Every Square Is a Rectangle
lessons.mainIdea: Shapes form a hierarchy: a shape that meets the rule for a group belongs to that group and to every bigger group above it.
reading: Here is a puzzle. Is a square a rectangle? A rectangle is a quadrilateral with four right angles. A square has four right angles. So yes, a square is a rectangle. It is a special rectangle whose sides all happen to be equal. But a rectangle is not always a square, because a rectangle's sides can be different lengths. This is a *hierarchy*: groups inside groups, like dogs inside mammals inside animals.

Read the family tree from the top. All quadrilaterals. Inside them, parallelograms, with two pairs of parallel sides. Inside parallelograms, rectangles (four right angles) and rhombuses (four equal sides). Where rectangles and rhombuses overlap sits the square. So a square is a rhombus, a rectangle, a parallelogram and a quadrilateral, all at once. Any *property* of every parallelogram, like opposite sides being equal, is also true of every square.

Test yourself with the words always, sometimes and never. A square is always a rectangle. A rectangle is sometimes a square. A rhombus is sometimes a rectangle, when it is a square. A trapezoid with only one pair of parallel sides is never a parallelogram. The most common mistake is reading the hierarchy backward and saying every rectangle is a square. Check the rule. Does every rectangle have four equal sides? No. So the claim is false.

words.d: groups inside bigger groups; a shape in a small group also belongs to every group above it
a fact that is true of a shape, like having four right angles or two pairs of parallel sides

look.title: The Shape Sorter Machine
look.text: Imagine a machine with three gates. Gate 1 asks: two pairs of parallel sides? Gate 2 asks: four right angles? Gate 3 asks: four equal sides? A shape passes a gate only if the answer is yes. A square passes all three. A 3 by 5 rectangle passes Gate 1 and Gate 2 but stops at Gate 3. A rhombus with 60° corners passes Gate 1 and Gate 3 but stops at Gate 2.
look.prompt: Which gates does a parallelogram with unequal sides and no right angles pass? Can any shape pass Gate 2 and Gate 3 without being a square?

check.q: Which statement is always true?
check.why: A square has four right angles, which is the rule for rectangles, so every square is a rectangle.

check.q: A shape is a rhombus. Which is certain about it?
choices: It has only one pair of parallel sides
check.why: Every rhombus has two pairs of parallel sides, so every rhombus is a parallelogram.

check.q: Opposite sides of every parallelogram are equal. What does this tell you about a rectangle?
choices: Nothing, because rectangles are not parallelograms
All four of its sides are equal
Its opposite sides are equal too
check.why: A rectangle is a parallelogram, so it inherits the property: its opposite sides are equal.

lessons.title: Lines of Symmetry
lessons.mainIdea: A line of symmetry folds a shape onto itself so the two halves match exactly.
reading: Fold a paper heart down the middle. The two halves land exactly on top of each other. That fold is a *line of symmetry*. A shape is *symmetric* if you can fold it along a line and the halves match perfectly. The letter A has one line of symmetry, straight down the middle. The letter H has two, one up and down and one across. The letter F has none.

Count the lines of symmetry in common shapes. A rectangle that is not a square has 2: one through the middle of the long sides and one through the middle of the short sides. Its *diagonals* are not lines of symmetry. Fold along one and the corners stick out. A square has 4: two through the middles of the sides and two diagonals. An equilateral triangle has 3. An isosceles triangle has 1. A scalene triangle has 0.

Two mistakes are common. First, students draw a line that cuts a shape into two equal pieces and call it symmetry. Cutting a rectangle corner to corner makes two equal triangles, but the halves do not fold onto each other, so it is not a line of symmetry. Second, students forget to test diagonal lines. Test every line by folding, on real paper or in your mind. Symmetry shows up in butterflies, snowflakes, faces and buildings.

words.d: a line you can fold a shape along so the two halves match exactly
having at least one line of symmetry
a segment that joins two corners of a shape that are not next to each other

look.title: Lines of Symmetry in Shapes
look.prompt: For the shapes with all sides equal, how does the number of sides compare to the number of lines of symmetry? Predict the count for a regular pentagon, which has 5 equal sides.

check.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
check.why: A square folds onto itself along two middle lines and two diagonals, which is 4 lines.

check.q: A rectangle that is not a square is folded corner to corner. Is that fold a line of symmetry?
choices: No, because the two halves do not land on each other
Yes, because the two triangles are equal
Yes, because every diagonal is a line of symmetry
No, because rectangles have no symmetry
check.why: Equal pieces are not enough. The halves must match when folded, and a rectangle's diagonal fold leaves corners sticking out.

check.q: Which letter has exactly one line of symmetry?
check.why: T folds onto itself along an up-and-down line only. H has two lines, and F and N have none.

lessons.title: Drawing the Other Half
lessons.mainIdea: To finish a symmetric shape, copy each corner the same distance from the line on the other side.
reading: Half of a shape is drawn on grid paper, with a line of symmetry down the middle. To finish it, take each corner of the half and count its distance from the line. Then mark a matching point, its *mirror point*, the same distance away on the other side. If a corner is 3 squares left of the line and 2 squares up, its mirror point is 3 squares right of the line and 2 squares up. Connect the mirror points in the same order.

Example. The line of symmetry runs up and down. The half shape has corners at 1 square left and 0 up, 4 squares left and 0 up, and 1 square left and 5 up. The mirror points are 1 right and 0 up, 4 right and 0 up, and 1 right and 5 up. Draw the whole shape and you get a symmetric figure like a wide arrowhead. Fold along the line in your mind. Every corner meets its twin.

Common mistake: copying the half by sliding it over instead of flipping it. A slide keeps a shape facing the same way. A flip turns it around, like a *reflection* in a mirror. Points close to the line stay close, and points far from the line stay far. Another mistake: measuring from the edge of the paper instead of from the line of symmetry. Always measure from the line.

words.d: the matching point on the other side of a line of symmetry, the same distance from the line
a flip across a line; the image is the same shape facing the opposite way

look.title: Finish the Butterfly
look.text: A butterfly's left wing is drawn with its body along an up-and-down line of symmetry. The wing's tip is 6 squares left of the body and 4 squares up. A spot on the wing is 2 squares left and 1 square up. Reflect each point across the body line to draw the right wing.
look.prompt: Where is the right wing's tip? Where is the matching spot? What stays the same and what changes when you reflect a point?

check.q: A point is 5 squares left of an up-and-down line of symmetry and 3 squares up. Where is its mirror point?
check.why: Reflecting across an up-and-down line changes left to right but keeps the height, so the mirror point is 5 right, 3 up.

check.q: A point sits right on the line of symmetry. Where is its mirror point?
choices: on the far edge of the paper
check.why: A point on the line is 0 squares away, so its mirror point is 0 squares away on the other side: the same spot.

check.q: Which move makes the other half of a symmetric shape?
check.why: Symmetry is a reflection, which is a flip across the line.

review.q: Which figure goes on forever in both directions?
review.why: A line has no endpoints, so it keeps going both ways. A segment has two endpoints and a ray has one.

review.q: An angle of exactly 90° is called
review.why: 90° is a square corner, which is a right angle.

review.q: A straight 180° angle is split into a 65° angle and one other angle. What is the other angle?
A triangle has three 60° angles and every side is 4 cm. What kind of triangle is it?
review.why: All three sides are equal, so it is equilateral, and 60 + 60 + 60 = 180 checks.

review.q: Which shape must have four right angles?
review.why: Four right angles is the rule that defines a rectangle. The others may or may not have them.
A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides, and a square has four equal sides, so every square is a rhombus.

review.q: Lines that cross at right angles are
How many lines of symmetry does an equilateral triangle have?
review.why: Each line runs from a corner to the middle of the opposite side, and there are three corners.

chapters.title: The Coordinate Plane and Patterns
chapters.bigQuestion: How can two numbers tell you exactly where something is, and what does a pattern look like when you graph it?

story.title: The X at (7, 4)
story.kicker: A treasure map with no trees, no rivers and no landmarks, only a grid and one pair of numbers.
paragraphs: On the last day of camp, the counselor hands each cabin a folded map. There are no trees, no rivers and no big rocks drawn on it. There is only a grid of squares, numbers along the bottom edge, numbers up the left edge, and a note: the X is at (7, 4).

Jamal's cabin argues. Does 7 mean seven steps up or seven steps over? Priya says the first number always means across, because you read a map the way you read a sentence, left to right first. They start at the corner where both edges read 0. They count 7 squares to the right, then 4 squares up, and put a finger on that spot.

Another cabin starts at the same corner, counts 4 to the right and 7 up, and digs in the wrong place. The order of the numbers matters. (7, 4) and (4, 7) are two different spots on the map. The corner where the numbers start, the point (0, 0), is where every trip begins.

Jamal's cabin paces it out in the field. Each square on the map is 10 steps. They walk 70 steps east and 40 steps north and find a box of snacks under a flat stone. On the way back, Priya notices something. Her count of steps makes a pattern: 10, 20, 30, 40. Numbers that grow by the same amount each time make a straight row of dots when you plot them. The grid is not just for treasure. It is a way to draw any pattern.
story.think: Why does the order of the two numbers in (7, 4) matter? What could go wrong if a map did not say which number comes first?

lessons.title: Ordered Pairs
lessons.mainIdea: An ordered pair (x, y) tells you first how far to go right, then how far to go up, starting from (0, 0).
reading: A *coordinate plane* is a grid made by two number lines that cross at a right angle. The line going across is the *x-axis*. The line going up is the y-axis. They cross at a point called the *origin*, labeled (0, 0). In this chapter we use only the part of the grid where both numbers are 0 or bigger. That part is called the first quadrant.

Every point on the grid has an address made of two numbers, called an *ordered pair*. The first number is the x-coordinate: how many units to move right from the origin. The second number is the y-coordinate: how many units to move up. To find (3, 5), start at the origin, move 3 right, then 5 up. Say it as 'over 3, up 5'. The x comes first, just as x comes before y in the alphabet.

The order is the whole point. (3, 5) and (5, 3) are different spots. (3, 5) is over 3 and up 5. (5, 3) is over 5 and up 3. Common mistake: reading the y first because the y-axis stands up tall. Another: mixing up points on the axes. (4, 0) sits on the x-axis, 4 units right and 0 up. (0, 4) sits on the y-axis, 0 right and 4 up. The origin, (0, 0), is where you always begin.

words.d: a grid made by two number lines, the x-axis and the y-axis, crossing at a right angle
the number line that runs across the coordinate plane; the first number in a pair is measured along it
the point (0, 0) where the two axes cross; every count starts there
two numbers in order, (x, y), that name one point: over x, then up y

look.title: Two Cabins, Two Spots
look.text: Cabin A reads the note (7, 4) as over 7, up 4. Cabin B reads it as over 4, up 7. Both start at the origin. Cabin A ends 7 units right and 4 units up. Cabin B ends 4 units right and 7 units up. On the grid, Cabin A's spot is farther to the right and lower. Cabin B's spot is farther to the left and higher.
look.prompt: Which cabin read the ordered pair correctly? How far apart, going across, are the two spots? How far apart going up?

check.q: To plot (2, 6), start at the origin and
check.why: The first number is x (right), the second is y (up): right 2, up 6.

check.q: Which point lies on the x-axis?
check.why: A point on the x-axis has gone up 0, so its y-coordinate is 0: (5, 0).

check.q: What is the ordered pair for the origin?
check.why: The origin is where the axes cross, with no movement right or up: (0, 0).

lessons.title: Plotting and Naming Points
lessons.mainIdea: To name a point, read straight down to the x-axis first, then straight across to the y-axis.
reading: To *plot* is to go from numbers to a dot. To name is to go from a dot to numbers. To name a point, put your finger on it. Slide straight down to the x-axis and read that number: the x-coordinate. Go back to the point and slide straight left to the y-axis: the y-coordinate. Write them as (x, y). A dot that is 6 over and 2 up is named (6, 2).

Plot these four points and connect them in order: A (1, 1), B (5, 1), C (5, 4), D (1, 4), then back to A. A and B are both 1 up, so segment AB is flat, or *horizontal*. B and C are both 5 over, so BC goes straight up; it is *vertical*. The shape is a rectangle, 4 units wide and 3 units tall. When two points share a y-coordinate, the segment between them is horizontal. When they share an x-coordinate, it is vertical.

Common mistakes when naming: counting the grid lines instead of the spaces, or starting the count at 1 instead of 0. The origin is 0, and the first line to the right of it is 1. Another mistake: reading a label above the point instead of below it, when a grid labels only the bottom axis. Always trace down to the x-axis and left to the y-axis, in that order.

words.d: to mark a point on the grid from its ordered pair
running across, level with the x-axis, like the horizon
running straight up and down, like the y-axis

look.title: Corners of a Rectangle
look.cite: Points A, B and C from the reading
look.prompt: Point D is straight above A and straight left of C. What are its coordinates? How wide and how tall is the rectangle ABCD?

check.q: A dot is 3 units right of the origin and 7 units up. Its name is
check.why: Right comes first, then up: (3, 7).

check.q: Points (2, 5) and (9, 5) are connected. The segment is
check.why: The same y-coordinate means the same height, so the segment runs flat across.

check.q: When naming a point, what do you read first?
choices: the number to its left on the y-axis
the number straight below it on the x-axis
check.why: The x-coordinate comes first, and you find it by tracing straight down to the x-axis.

lessons.title: Distances Along the Grid
lessons.mainIdea: If two points share a coordinate, the distance between them is the difference of the other coordinates.
reading: How far is it from (2, 3) to (9, 3)? Both points are 3 up, so they sit on the same horizontal line. Count the squares between them, or just subtract the x-coordinates: 9 − 2 = 7 units. Now try (4, 1) to (4, 10). Same x, so the points are on a vertical line. Subtract the y-coordinates: 10 − 1 = 9 units. The *distance* is the *difference* of the coordinates that are not the same.

For a trip that turns a corner, add the legs. From (1, 2) go to (6, 2), then up to (6, 8). First leg: 6 − 1 = 5. Second leg: 8 − 2 = 6. Total: 5 + 6 = 11 units. On a city grid, this is how far you walk when you cannot cut through buildings. If each unit is one block, that trip is 11 blocks.

Common mistake: subtracting the wrong pair. From (2, 3) to (9, 3), a student computes 9 − 3 = 6, mixing an x with a y. Always subtract x from x or y from y. Another mistake: counting grid lines instead of spaces, which gives one too many. From 2 to 9 there are 7 spaces, not 8. Check with a tiny case: from 2 to 3 is 1 space, and 3 − 2 = 1.

words.d: how far apart two points are, measured in grid units
the answer to a subtraction; the larger coordinate minus the smaller one

look.title: Walking the Blocks
look.text: On a grid of city blocks, the library is at (3, 8) and the school is at (3, 2). A student walks from the school straight to the library. Both points have x = 3, so the walk is vertical: 8 − 2 = 6 blocks. After the library, the student walks to a park at (10, 8). Both of those points have y = 8, so this leg is horizontal.
look.prompt: How long is the second leg? How many blocks is the whole trip from the school to the park by way of the library?

check.q: What is the distance from (5, 6) to (5, 1)?
check.why: Same x, so subtract the y-coordinates: 6 − 1 = 5.

check.q: What is the distance from (1, 4) to (8, 4)?
check.why: Same y, so subtract the x-coordinates: 8 − 1 = 7.

check.q: A path goes from (0, 0) to (6, 0), then to (6, 5). How long is the whole path?
check.why: 6 + 5 = 11. Multiplying 6 × 5 would give an area, not a distance.

lessons.title: Graphing a Pattern
lessons.mainIdea: A pattern becomes a set of points when you pair each step number with its value.
reading: Marta saves $3 every week. After 1 week she has $3, after 2 weeks $6, after 3 weeks $9, after 4 weeks $12. Make a *table* with two columns: week and dollars. Now turn each row into an ordered pair: (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 12). Plot them, with weeks on the x-axis and dollars on the y-axis. The points march up in a straight line.

Why a straight line? Each step right (one more week) goes up the same amount (3 dollars). A *pattern* that adds the same number each time always plots as points in a straight line. The steeper the line, the bigger the number being added. Saving $5 a week would make a steeper line: (1, 5), (2, 10), (3, 15). Saving $1 a week would make a line that is nearly flat.

Read the graph backward too. A point at (6, 18) says: after 6 weeks, $18. To find the amount after 10 weeks, *extend* the pattern: 10 × 3 = 30, the point (10, 30). Common mistake: swapping the axes and plotting (3, 1) for week 1. Put the week first, because it is what you choose, and the dollars depend on it. Another mistake: drawing a solid line when only whole weeks make sense. Points are enough.

words.d: rows and columns of numbers; here, one column for the step and one for its value
a list of numbers made by a rule, like adding 3 each time
to continue a pattern past the numbers you were given

look.title: Marta's Savings
look.prompt: What ordered pair goes with week 8? If Marta wants $45, in which week does she reach it?

check.q: A pattern adds 4 each step, starting at 4. Which ordered pair belongs to it?
check.why: Step 3 has value 4 × 3 = 12, so the pair is (3, 12): step first, value second.

check.q: Which pattern makes the steepest line of points?
check.why: The bigger the amount added, the more each point rises, so adding 5 is steepest.

check.q: The point (7, 21) is on the graph of a savings pattern. What does it mean?
check.why: The x-coordinate is the week and the y-coordinate is the dollars: 7 weeks, $21.

lessons.title: Two Patterns Side by Side
lessons.mainIdea: When two patterns start at 0 and one adds twice as much, every value in the second is twice the matching value in the first.
reading: Start two patterns at 0. Pattern A adds 3 each step: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12. Pattern B adds 6 each step: 0, 6, 12, 18, 24. Line them up. Step 1: 3 and 6. Step 2: 6 and 12. Step 3: 9 and 18. Each B value is exactly double the *corresponding* A value. That makes sense. B adds twice as much every time, so after any number of steps B has twice as much.

Now graph the pairs (A, B): (0, 0), (3, 6), (6, 12), (9, 18). These points also fall in a straight line, and every point has a y that is twice its x. Try another pair. Pattern C adds 2: 0, 2, 4, 6. Pattern D adds 10: 0, 10, 20, 30. Each D value is 5 times the matching C value, because 10 is 5 times 2.

Common mistake: saying B is always 3 more than A. That is only true at step 1. At step 4, A is 12 and B is 24, a difference of 12, not 3. The *relationship* that stays true at every step is that B is 2 times A. Ask: what do I multiply A by to get B? If the patterns do not both start at 0, the rule is different, so check the starting numbers first.

words.d: matching; the values from two patterns that sit at the same step
a rule that connects the corresponding values of two patterns, like 'B is twice A'

look.title: Add 3 Versus Add 6
look.cite: Pattern A adds 3, pattern B adds 6, both starting at 0
look.prompt: What is A at step 10? What is B at step 10? What single rule connects every pair of values?

check.q: Pattern A adds 4 each step from 0. Pattern B adds 8 each step from 0. At step 5, what are A and B?
check.why: A: 4 × 5 = 20. B: 8 × 5 = 40, which is double.

check.q: Two patterns start at 0. One adds 2, the other adds 10. Each value in the second pattern is
check.why: 10 is 5 times 2, so at every step the second pattern has 5 times as much.

check.q: Which is true at every step for A (add 3) and B (add 6), both starting at 0?
check.why: At step 1 the values are 3 and 6; at step 4 they are 12 and 24. Only 'B is twice A' holds every time.

lessons.title: Rules That Add
lessons.mainIdea: An add rule tells you the start and what to add; to find any term, apply the rule step by step or count the jumps.
reading: A *rule* is an instruction that makes a pattern. 'Start at 5, add 4' gives 5, 9, 13, 17, 21. Each number is a *term*. The first term is 5. To get the next term, add 4. To find the 6th term, keep going: 21 + 4 = 25. Or count the jumps: five jumps of 4 after the start. 5 + 5 × 4 = 5 + 20 = 25. Either way, the 6th term is 25.

Rules can subtract too. 'Start at 50, subtract 7' gives 50, 43, 36, 29, 22. Check: 43 − 7 = 36, and 36 − 7 = 29. The terms go down by the same amount each time. To find a rule from a pattern, subtract neighbors. In 8, 14, 20, 26, each gap is the same: 14 − 8 = 6, 20 − 14 = 6, 26 − 20 = 6. Rule: start at 8, add 6.

Common mistakes: forgetting the start, so 'start at 5, add 4' turns into 4, 8, 12. Or adding one extra jump: the 6th term has 5 jumps after the first term, not 6. Count the jumps on your fingers. Term 1 to term 2 is one jump. Another mistake when finding a rule: subtracting in the wrong order. Later term minus earlier term gives the gap.

words.d: an instruction that makes a pattern: where to start and what to do each step
one number in a pattern; the 1st term is the start

look.title: The Stair Pattern
look.text: A staircase is built from blocks. Step 1 uses 4 blocks. Each new step uses 3 more blocks than the one before. So step 2 uses 7, step 3 uses 10 and step 4 uses 13. Rule: start at 4, add 3. To find step 8, count 7 jumps of 3 after the start: 4 + 7 × 3 = 4 + 21 = 25 blocks.
look.prompt: How many blocks does step 6 use? Which step uses exactly 34 blocks? Show the jumps.

check.q: Rule: start at 6, add 5. What is the 4th term?
check.why: 6, 11, 16, 21. Three jumps of 5 after 6: 6 + 15 = 21.

check.q: Pattern: 30, 26, 22, 18. What is the rule?
check.why: Each term is 4 less than the one before: 30 − 4 = 26, 26 − 4 = 22, 22 − 4 = 18.

check.q: Rule: start at 2, add 9. What is the 10th term?
check.why: Nine jumps after the start: 2 + 9 × 9 = 2 + 81 = 83.

lessons.title: Rules That Multiply
lessons.mainIdea: A multiply rule grows faster and faster, because each term is a multiple of the one before.
reading: 'Start at 1, multiply by 2' gives 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Each term is *double* the one before. Compare that with 'start at 1, add 2', which gives 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. The add pattern climbs steadily. The multiply pattern climbs slowly at first and then races ahead. By the 6th term, the doubling pattern is at 32 while the add pattern is at 11. Folding paper gets thick so fast for the same reason. Each fold doubles the layers.

To find a multiply rule from a pattern, divide neighbors. In 3, 12, 48, 192: 12 ÷ 3 = 4, 48 ÷ 12 = 4, 192 ÷ 48 = 4. Rule: start at 3, multiply by 4. Every term is a *multiple* of the one before it. Check the next term: 192 × 4 = 768. Rules can divide too. 'Start at 80, divide by 2' gives 80, 40, 20, 10, 5.

On a graph, an add pattern makes points in a straight line. A multiply pattern makes points that curve upward, getting steeper. Common mistake: testing only the first gap. In 2, 4, 8 a student sees 4 − 2 = 2 and says 'add 2'. But 8 − 4 = 4, not 2. Check at least two gaps. Then try division: 4 ÷ 2 = 2 and 8 ÷ 4 = 2. The rule is multiply by 2.

words.d: two times as much; 8 is double 4
a number you get by multiplying; 12 is a multiple of 3 because 3 × 4 = 12

look.title: Start at 1, Multiply by 2
look.prompt: What is term 10 of this pattern? What would term 10 be for 'start at 1, add 2' instead? Which is bigger, and by how much?

check.q: Rule: start at 5, multiply by 3. What is the 4th term?
check.why: 5, 15, 45, 135. Three multiplications by 3 after the start.

check.q: Pattern: 2, 6, 18, 54. What is the rule?
check.why: 6 ÷ 2 = 3, 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 54 ÷ 18 = 3, so each term is 3 times the one before.

check.q: How can you tell a multiply pattern from an add pattern on a graph?
choices: Multiply patterns make a straight line
Multiply patterns curve upward, getting steeper
check.why: Add patterns rise the same amount each step and make a line. Multiply patterns rise more each step and make a curve.

lessons.title: Describing a Pattern's Features
lessons.mainIdea: Look beyond the rule: notice whether terms are odd or even, what digit they end in, and why that must happen.
reading: Once you have a pattern, describe what you notice. Rule: start at 3, add 3. Terms: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18. Notice that the terms switch between *odd* and *even*. Every term is a multiple of 3. Every other term is a multiple of 6. These are *features* of the pattern that the rule does not say out loud, but you can explain them. Adding 3 to an odd number gives an even number, and adding 3 to an even number gives an odd number. So the terms must alternate.

Rule: start at 4, add 4. Terms: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. Every term is even. Why? 4 is even, and even plus even is always even, so the pattern can never reach an odd number. Rule: start at 5, add 10. Terms: 5, 15, 25, 35. Every term ends in 5. Why? Adding 10 changes the tens digit but never the ones digit.

Common mistake: describing only the first few terms. 'The terms are less than 20' is true for 4, 8, 12, 16 but false for 20. A good feature holds for every term, and you can say why. Another mistake: saying two patterns are the same because they share a few numbers. 'Add 3' and 'add 6' both contain 6 and 12, but they are different patterns with different rules.

words.d: something true about every term of a pattern, like 'all the terms are even'
a whole number that can be split into two equal whole parts: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and so on
a whole number that is not even: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and so on

look.title: Odd or Even Forever
look.text: Rule: start at 7, add 2. Terms: 7, 9, 11, 13, 15. Every term is odd. Reason: 7 is odd, and adding 2, an even number, keeps a number odd. Now change the start. Rule: start at 6, add 2. Terms: 6, 8, 10, 12. Every term is even. Finally, rule: start at 6, add 5. Terms: 6, 11, 16, 21, 26.
look.prompt: Describe the odd-and-even feature of the 'start at 6, add 5' pattern, and explain why it happens.

check.q: Rule: start at 2, add 2. Which feature is true of every term?
check.why: 2 is even and adding 2 keeps it even, so the pattern 2, 4, 6, 8 and beyond is all even.

check.q: Rule: start at 10, add 10. What digit does every term end in?
check.why: 10, 20, 30, 40: adding 10 never changes the ones digit, which stays 0.

check.q: Rule: start at 1, add 3. Terms: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13. Which describes the odd-and-even feature?
check.why: Adding an odd number flips odd to even and back: 1 odd, 4 even, 7 odd, 10 even.

lessons.title: Maps and Coordinates
lessons.mainIdea: Real maps use coordinate ideas: a starting point, a direction across, a direction up, and distances you find by subtracting.
reading: Chicago's street addresses work like a coordinate plane. The origin is the corner of State Street and Madison Street downtown. State Street splits the city into east and west. Madison Street splits it into north and south. An *address* number grows as you move away from that corner. In most of the city, 800 address numbers equal about 1 mile. So an address of 1600 North is about 2 miles north of Madison Street.

Put a simple town on a *grid*. Each unit is 1 block. The school is at (2, 3), the library at (2, 9) and the pool at (8, 9). School to library: same x, so 9 − 3 = 6 blocks north. Library to pool: same y, so 8 − 2 = 6 blocks east. A walk from the school to the pool by way of the library is 6 + 6 = 12 blocks. Coordinates turn a map question into subtraction.

Grids show up in other places too. A spreadsheet names each *cell* by a column letter and a row number, like B4. A chessboard names each square the same way, from a1 to h8. In the game Battleship, you call out a letter and a number. Common mistake with real grids: forgetting which direction comes first. A chessboard reads column then row, just like (x, y). Check the labels before you count.

words.d: the number and street that name a place; in Chicago the numbers count away from State and Madison
a set of evenly spaced lines that cross, making squares you can count
one box in a spreadsheet, named by its column letter and row number

look.title: Chicago's Grid
look.text: Downtown Chicago's corner of State and Madison is the city's origin, its (0, 0). A shop is at 800 North on a north-south street, about 1 mile north of Madison. A friend lives at 2400 North, about 3 miles north. Both are north of the origin, so subtract the miles: 3 − 1 = 2 miles apart going north.
look.prompt: A park sits at 4000 North. About how many miles is it north of Madison Street? About how far is it from the shop at 800 North?

check.q: On a town grid, the bakery is at (4, 2) and the bank is at (4, 11). How many blocks apart are they?
check.why: Same x, so subtract the y-coordinates: 11 − 2 = 9 blocks.

check.q: In Chicago, about 800 address numbers make 1 mile. About how far from Madison Street is 3200 North?
A chessboard square is named e4. Which part comes first, like the x in (x, y)?
check.why: Chess names the column (across) first and the row (up) second, the same order as an ordered pair.

lessons.title: Shapes on the Grid
lessons.mainIdea: Plot the vertices, connect them, and use coordinates to find side lengths, missing corners and the perimeter.
reading: Plot A (2, 1), B (7, 1) and C (7, 4). Connect them and you have a right triangle. Side AB is horizontal: 7 − 2 = 5 units. Side BC is vertical: 4 − 1 = 3 units. The right angle is at B, the *vertex* where the horizontal and vertical sides meet. Coordinates let you find lengths without a ruler, as long as the sides run along grid lines.

Find a missing corner. Three corners of a rectangle are (1, 2), (6, 2) and (6, 5). The fourth corner must be straight above (1, 2) and straight left of (6, 5). So it shares x = 1 with the first point and y = 5 with the third: (1, 5). The rectangle is 6 − 1 = 5 units wide and 5 − 2 = 3 units tall. Its *perimeter*, the distance all the way around, is 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 units.

Common mistake: picking a missing corner because it looks about right. Use the shared coordinates instead. Another mistake: finding the width as 6 + 1 instead of 6 − 1. The width is a difference. Also remember that a slanted side, like the side from A to C in the triangle, cannot be found by subtracting coordinates. Only horizontal and vertical sides work that way.

words.d: a corner of a shape, where two sides meet; the plural is vertices
the distance all the way around a shape, found by adding the side lengths

look.title: The Garden Plot
look.text: A community garden in a city park is drawn on a grid where each unit is 1 meter. Its corners are (3, 2), (11, 2), (11, 8) and (3, 8). Width: 11 − 3 = 8 m. Height: 8 − 2 = 6 m. A fence goes all the way around: 8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28 m. Now the gardeners want more room.
look.prompt: They move the corners (11, 2) and (11, 8) so that x = 15 for both. What are the new width and the new fence length?

check.q: Three corners of a rectangle are (2, 3), (8, 3) and (8, 7). What is the fourth corner?
check.why: It shares x = 2 with (2, 3) and y = 7 with (8, 7), so it is (2, 7).

check.q: A rectangle has corners (0, 0), (9, 0), (9, 4) and (0, 4). What is its perimeter?
check.why: Width 9, height 4: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26. The number 36 is the area, not the perimeter.

check.q: Points (1, 1), (6, 1) and (6, 3) make a triangle. How long is the horizontal side?
check.why: From (1, 1) to (6, 1) the y is the same, so the length is 6 − 1 = 5.

review.q: Which point is 4 units right and 9 units up from the origin?
review.why: Right comes first and up comes second: (4, 9).

review.q: What is the distance from (3, 2) to (3, 12)?
review.why: Same x, so subtract the y-coordinates: 12 − 2 = 10.

review.q: Rule: start at 7, add 6. What is the 5th term?

review.why: 10 ÷ 5 = 2, 20 ÷ 10 = 2, 40 ÷ 20 = 2. The gaps 5, 10, 20 are not equal, so it is not an add rule.

review.q: Pattern A adds 5 from 0 and pattern B adds 10 from 0. At every step, B is
review.why: Step 1: 5 and 10. Step 3: 15 and 30. B is always 2 times A.

review.q: Which point lies on the y-axis?
review.why: A point on the y-axis has moved 0 to the right, so its x-coordinate is 0.

review.q: Three corners of a rectangle are (2, 2), (10, 2) and (10, 5). What is the fourth corner?
review.why: It shares x = 2 with (2, 2) and y = 5 with (10, 5).

review.q: Rule: start at 4, add 4. Which is true of every term?
choices: every term is a multiple of 3
review.why: 4 is even and even plus even is even, so 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and beyond are all even.
